title: Intrinsic motivation
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: What does each person on your team really want, and do you know?

Jose said that with children we are drawn to give extrinsic motivation: if you do this, you get a cookie, a hundred dollars for good grades. We are constantly bribing our kids. As adults we are surrounded by extrinsic motivation: if you do this you will make more money.

What is different with these entrepreneurs, he said, is that they are motivated by intrinsic things. That is why they are mission-oriented. That is where the passion and the innovation come from. Money is a byproduct to them, a consequence.

As a leader, he said, you want to read everything you can about intrinsic motivation. If a person hasn't grown up with it in childhood, you will be teaching it from the ground up. Extrinsic is just a band-aid.

Jose told how, when his children competed and were little, they would be on the plane flying to compete, and he would say: you are already champions. You've already won because you had the discipline and trained for six months. Anything that happens after this is irrelevant.

A student said: as a leader you have to figure out what motivates people. A lot of people think it is money. It motivates many people for different reasons: recognition, a job well done, extra days off, time on a project. If you tap into each person's motivation you bring out the intrinsic motivation, the most effective there is.

Extrinsic doesn't mean it doesn't help, Jose said. When I take a big group to a restaurant, I immediately approach the waiter: these people are very important to me and I want to make it a remarkable night. We are going to be a team. In two or three minutes I have established a little trust.
Encouragement is a big part of this, he said. He called the person in the book a fear-driven leader, who doesn't know encouragement because he did not grow up with it.

A student said: if he uses fear, that will work for some people but it is generally not effective. In your example with the waiter you say: I know you will do a great job, we are a team. That puts you on his level or elevates him to yours, and he won't want to let you down.
What would you say to the waiter in your team?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write what motivates each person on your team.
Write which of those is extrinsic and which intrinsic.
Write one thing you could say to show faith in someone.
Write how you would begin a first meeting as a team.
Write what you praise: the result or the discipline behind it.

check.q: What did Jose call extrinsic motivation?
What did a student say about what motivates people?
What did Jose do at the restaurant?
choices: Established trust with the waiter in two or three minutes

recap: Find each person's intrinsic motivation. Show faith in them. Extrinsic rewards alone are a band-aid.
